name: Hick's Law
description: The time to make a decision increases with the number and complexity of choices available.
design_relevance_note: The direct academic backing for 'reduce the number of choices/menu items' design advice.
myth_risk_note: Law is well-supported for pure choice-reaction time tasks but HCI applicability is questioned; Liu et al. argue the assumption that fewer interface options reduce decision time may not hold when choice-reaction time is constant or involves visual search and decision-making processes orthogonal to stimulus-response mapping.
prevalence_note: Taught alongside Fitts's Law as a foundational interaction-design principle — choice count and decision time are a standard UI design consideration.

findings.description: Choice reaction time increases with the number of stimulus-response alternatives (or amount of decision uncertainty) in a task — a robust, widely-replicated relationship, though with documented boundary conditions (stimulus-response compatibility effects, practice effects, and challenges at very large numbers of alternatives).
findings.source_title: Hick's law for choice reaction time: A review

applications.title: Twitter's simplified logged-out homepage: fewer choices, faster decisions
applications.description: Smashing Magazine's 2012 analysis of Hick's Law observed that Twitter had progressively reduced the number of choices on its logged-out homepage over time, narrowing it down to essentially sign-up and log-in, compared to the more option-heavy homepage it had presented in earlier years -- framed as an application of Hick's Law beyond simple navigation-menu length.
applications.ethical_note: Reducing genuinely unnecessary choices to ease cognitive load is user-beneficial on its face, but when the specific choices removed are the ones that would let a visitor do anything other than sign up, the same simplification also functions as a conversion funnel narrowing toward one outcome -- graded mixed because the source doesn't let us cleanly separate 'reducing user overwhelm' from 'reducing paths away from sign-up.'
